summary: This informational memo discusses vendor extensions to PPP, the Point-to-Point Protocol, which carries multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links using LCP and NCPs. It provides information for the community and is not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is used to carry data over a direct link between two devices, and it has its own rules for setting up and managing that link. Sometimes a vendor needs to add something private that is not in the standard. This memo gives vendors one shared slot to do that: a code that marks a message as vendor-specific, plus the vendor's registered identifier and its own sub-type, so different vendors never clash and IANA does not have to hand out numbers for every private feature.

questions: what is the ppp vendor specific packet
what is an oui in ppp
what is the cf0000 oui series
subtitle: A standard way for vendors to add their own private packets and options to the Point-to-Point Protocol without asking IANA for numbers.

tldr.problem: PPP implements Link Control Protocol and network control protocols, but vendors sometimes need private algorithms and attributes. Without a common mechanism they would request many private code and type numbers from IANA or collide with each other.
tldr.mechanism: It reserves code 0 in control packets and type 0 in configuration options for vendor-specific use, and puts a vendor's Organizationally Unique Identifier and a Kind sub-type in the message so each vendor controls its own meaning.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC from May 1997 that updates RFC 1661 and RFC 1962, and it has since been updated by RFC 5342 and RFC 7042.

today: RFC 2153 is an Informational RFC published in May 1997. It updates RFC 1661 and RFC 1962, and has been updated by RFC 5342 and RFC 7042, which deal with IANA considerations and the registration of IEEE identifiers.

sections.title: Vendor-Specific Control Packets
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol provides a standard method for carrying multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links. PPP defines an extensible Link Control Protocol (LCP) for establishing, configuring and testing the data-link connection, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for establishing and configuring different network-layer protocols. This memo defines a general mechanism for proprietary vendor extensions to those control protocols.

Some implementors may not need or want to publish their proprietary algorithms and attributes. The mechanism lets them specify these things without burdening IANA with requests for proprietary numbers. When the code field of an LCP or NCP packet is set to 0, the packet is vendor-specific: the sender fills in the identifier, inserts the local Magic-Number if there is one, sets the OUI and Kind fields, and puts any desired data in the value field.

Vendor-specific packets may be sent at any time, including before LCP has reached the Opened state. Each packet sent must use a fresh identifier. The receiver's response is up to the vendor, and the value field must not exceed the default maximum receive unit minus twelve.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages that manage a PPP link can carry a special code, the number zero, meaning this message is private to a particular vendor. The sender says who it is and what kind of private message this is, and the rest of the message holds whatever that vendor defines.

sections.title: Organizationally Unique Identifiers
sections.content:
The three-octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) identifies the organization that administers the meaning of the message, and it is based on IEEE 802 vendor assignments. A vendor that wants to use its existing IEEE 802 OUI for PPP vendor extensions should also register that OUI with IANA. A vendor that does not otherwise need an IEEE-assigned number can instead request a PPP-specific OUI from IANA, assigned from the CF0000 series.

That CF0000 series has both the locally assigned and the broadcast or multicast bits set to one, that is, the least significant two bits of the most significant octet are both one. The choice of CF0000 is a mnemonic convenience, chosen to match the PPP NLPID CF. The reasoning is that multicast has no meaning in PPP, so an IEEE-assigned OUI would have the multicast bit cleared, making a set multicast bit a clear mark of a locally assigned value. The RFC also notes that it is not clear how IEEE assigns blocks and that the locally assigned bit is known to have been used in some cases.

Inside the packet, the OUI's bits are in canonical order and the most significant octet is transmitted first.
sections.plainLanguage: Each vendor is named by a three-byte identifier that normally comes from the IEEE, the same kind of identifier used for hardware addresses. A vendor with no such number can get one from IANA instead, from a range whose first byte marks it as locally assigned. The bytes are sent most significant first.

sections.title: Packet Layout and Configuration Options
sections.content:
The vendor-specific packet begins with the usual Code, Identifier and Length fields of a control packet. The Length must be at least twelve, and when it is exactly twelve there is no value field. The Magic-Number is four octets and helps detect links that are looped back; until the Magic-Number Configuration Option has been successfully negotiated it must be transmitted as zero. The OUI is three octets and the Kind is one octet, and the Kind field may be extended by the vendor using zero or more octets of the value field. The value field is zero or more octets whose details are implementation specific.

The same idea applies to configuration options. The Option Type field value 0 marks a vendor-specific option, whose Length must be at least six, with no value field when the length is exactly six. Before accepting such an option an implementation must verify that the OUI and Kind specify a known mechanism and that any vendor-specific negotiation values are fully understood. Both mechanisms exist to avoid conflicts from vendors secretly assigning their own packet codes and option types.

The Kind field is what gives each vendor room to grow: because a vendor controls its own OUI, it can define as many kinds and as much value data as it needs, and the number zero in the standard fields keeps that private space from colliding with future standard extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with the normal PPP fields and then carries the vendor's identifier, a single byte saying which of that vendor's message types this is, and any data the vendor wants. The same pattern is used for link setup options, and a device must not accept an option unless it recognizes the vendor and the sub-type and understands the values.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states plainly that security issues are not discussed in this document. That brevity is worth noting rather than glossing over. The mechanism hands control of message meaning to each vendor, so the safeguards are the receiving implementation's own: it must confirm that an OUI and Kind identify a mechanism it knows and that the negotiation values are fully understood before acting on them. Because vendor-specific packets may arrive before LCP reaches the Opened state and may be sent at any time, a device must be prepared for them from either peer.

The document is a small extension to existing protocols rather than a standalone security protocol. It updates RFC 1661, the PPP specification, and RFC 1962, the compression control protocol, by adding this vendor-specific facility to their control packets and configuration options.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says nothing about security, which means the work of staying safe falls on the device itself: it should only act on vendor messages it recognizes and understands. The change itself just adds a private slot to rules that already existed.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 0 marks the packet as vendor specific.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: A new value for each packet sent.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: At least 12; 12 means no value data.
